stem: Which of the following is the interval notation for the set $\{x:x\in\mathbb{R},x{=sg}{=c}\}$?
solution: The set holds every real number that is {=dirw}{=eqw} ${=c}$, so it runs on without end {=way}. One end of the interval is therefore ${=infw}$.
Infinity is not a number and can never be reached or included, so the bracket next to it is always round.
The sign ${=sg}$ at ${=c}$ means ${=c}$ {=cin} the set, so the bracket next to ${=c}$ is {=cbn}.
Write the end on the left first: ${=lbc}{=loc}, {=hic}{=rbc}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Square bracket written next to infinity
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student treats infinity like an end number that can be included, so writes a square bracket next to it, as in $[-\infty, 5]$ or $[5, \infty]$. Infinity is not a number and always takes a round bracket.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Half-line written running the wrong way
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student writes the interval that starts at the end number and runs the opposite way along the number line, for example $[5, \infty)$ for $x \le 5$ or $(-\infty, 5]$ for $x \ge 5$, matching the bracket to the sign but mixing up which side of the number the set lies on.

notes: Advanced: the twist the book itself uses, one end at infinity (ex6-1-1a/c/f, ex6-1-2a). The side param picks x less than c or x greater than c. Three single-error distractors, always distinct from the correct option and from each other: the finite end's bracket flipped (existing id), a square bracket at infinity (proposed), the half-line reversed with the finite bracket kept (proposed). Unicode infinity and sign characters are used inside computed strings so no backslash sits in an expression string literal; please confirm the renderer shows them inside $...$. Option pieces are mixed string/number lists indexed by side; if the engine rejects mixed lists, the fix is mechanical.
